title: Va'era: why Aaron struck the river (Exodus 7:19)
hook: Rashi: Moses didn't strike the Nile because it once saved his life

segments.voice: Yesterday, Va'era: the people couldn't hear Moses, for shortness of breath and cruel bondage. Tired ears can't hear. Today, the first plague, and a strange detail about who strikes the water.

People get attached to strange things. The old car that got you through college. The bench in the hospital garden where you waited for news. The tree you climbed as a kid. You'd feel something if someone took a chainsaw to it, even though it's just wood, just metal. For Moses, the Nile isn't just a river. When he was three months old, his mother put him in a little basket, sealed it with pitch, and set it among the reeds. That water carried him to safety. And now God is about to turn the Nile to blood.
screen: `ATTACHED TO STRANGE THINGS.` → `A BABY IN A BASKET.` → `THE RIVER THAT CARRIED HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the detail. For the first plague, God doesn't tell Moses to strike the water. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Say unto Aaron: Take thy rod, and stretch out thy hand over the waters of Egypt." Aaron, not Moses. Why the switch? Moses is the one who spoke with God at the bush, and Moses carries the staff. Rashi, passing on an older midrash, gives the answer: the river protected Moses when he was thrown into it as a baby, so it wasn't right for him to be the one to strike it. The second plague, the frogs, comes up out of the river: Aaron again. The third, the lice, comes from striking the dust of the ground: Aaron again. Rashi says the dust protected Moses too. When he killed the Egyptian taskmaster, he hid the body in the sand. The earth kept his secret, so it, too, was spared his hand. It's an odd idea. A river doesn't know it saved anyone, and sand doesn't have feelings. The point isn't what the water feels. It's what Moses becomes if he can strike, without a second thought, the thing that saved him. The Talmud has a saying for this: a well you drank from, don't throw a clod of earth into it. Jewish tradition calls the trait hakarat hatov, recognizing the good. Not just saying thanks, but remembering, long after, who and what carried you.
screen: `SAY UNTO AARON: TAKE THY ROD.` · `THE RIVER SAVED THE BABY.` · `THE DUST KEPT HIS SECRET.` · `HAKARAT HATOV — RECOGNIZE THE GOOD.` · then, large: `GRATITUDE EVEN TO WATER.`

segments.voice: Think of something, not someone, that carried you through: a car that got you to the hospital in time, the library where you hid from a hard home, a song, a city, a bed, a coat. Picture it and thank it silently, even though it can't hear. Then ask yourself whether there's anything like it you've been treating carelessly lately.
Va'era. The portion of the first plagues, where Aaron strikes the Nile because, Rashi says, the river once saved Moses.
Your line: gratitude even to water. Before it ever turned to blood, the river carried him. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hakarat hatov, recognizing the good, is taught as a Jewish value; the Modeh Ani said on waking thanks God for returning the soul, and traditional blessings are said over food, water and ordinary moments.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 7:19 (the fragment quoted).
Rashi on 7:19 and 8:12 (river and dust protected Moses) from memory, drawing on Exodus Rabbah 9:10 / Tanchuma; confirm.
Bava Kamma 92b: 'a well you drank from, do not cast a clod into it'; the script says 'stone'; confirm wording.
Verse numbers for frogs and lice follow the Hebrew numbering (8:1, 8:12); English Bibles number them 8:5 and 8:16.
